cues.text: Welcome to the Mole Concept.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Begin with what a chemical equation is allowed to change.
In an ordinary chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged; the nuclei are not
converted into different elements.
For a closed system, total mass is conserved to the accuracy of ordinary
chemical measurements.
Gas escaping from an open vessel can make the measured vessel contents lighter
without violating conservation.
The law of definite proportions describes the fixed elemental mass ratio of a
specified pure compound.
Using rounded masses, water has hydrogen to oxygen mass ratio two to sixteen,
or one to eight.
Hydrogen peroxide is a different compound with a different ratio.
The law of multiple proportions compares different compounds formed from the
same two elements: for a fixed mass of one element, the other masses occur in
small whole number ratios.
Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide illustrate oxygen masses sixteen and thirty
two for carbon mass twelve.
Dalton's model helped explain these laws, but modern atoms have subatomic
structure and isotopes.
Distinguish a useful historical model from its later corrections.
A mole counts specified entities, just as a dozen counts twelve objects.
The Avogadro constant is exactly six point zero two two one four zero seven
six
times ten to the twenty three per mole.
For routine examples we will use six point zero two two times ten to the
twenty
three.
Always name the counted entity: atoms, molecules, ions or formula units.
One mole of oxygen molecules contains two moles of oxygen atoms.
One mole of sodium chloride solid describes formula units in a lattice, not a
collection of separate sodium chloride molecules.
Molar mass connects mass with amount: divide mass by molar mass to obtain
moles.
Using hydrogen one and oxygen sixteen grams per mole, water has molar mass
eighteen grams per mole.
Nine grams of water is therefore half a mole of molecules, or about three
point
zero one one times ten to the twenty three molecules.
That same sample contains one mole of hydrogen atoms and half a mole of oxygen
atoms.
A mole has a fixed entity count, but its mass depends on the substance.
Read every subscript before calculating formula mass.
Parentheses multiply the whole enclosed group.
Calcium hydroxide contains one calcium, two oxygen and two hydrogen atoms per
formula unit.
Using calcium forty, oxygen sixteen and hydrogen one, its formula mass is
forty
plus twice seventeen, or seventy four.
Its molar mass is seventy four grams per mole under those rounded assumptions.
Thus seven point four grams corresponds to zero point one mole of formula
units
and zero point two mole of hydroxide groups.
Counting these groups is not a claim that every solid sample is already
dissolved into free ions.
Percentage composition is the elemental mass contribution divided by total
formula mass, multiplied by one hundred.
For water, oxygen contributes sixteen out of eighteen, about eighty eight
point
nine percent by mass.
A relative molecular mass is dimensionless; the mass of one molecule may be
expressed in atomic mass units, while molar mass has units such as grams per
mole.
These quantities are related but should not be assigned interchangeable units.
Use the atomic masses given in the question.
An empirical formula gives the simplest whole number atom ratio.
A molecular formula gives the actual atom counts in one molecule.
Suppose a compound is forty point zero percent carbon, six point seven percent
hydrogen and fifty three point three percent oxygen by mass.
Assume one hundred grams.
Divide by the rounded atomic molar masses twelve, one and sixteen: the amounts
are approximately three point three three, six point seven and three point
three three moles.
Divide all by the smallest amount to obtain approximately one to two to one.
The empirical formula is C H two O.
Its formula mass is thirty.
If the measured molar mass is one hundred eighty grams per mole, the
multiplier
is six and the molecular formula is C six H twelve O six.
Percentage rounding explains small deviations from ideal integers.
Do not round one point five directly to two: multiply every ratio by two
instead.
Composition alone cannot distinguish all molecular formulas sharing the same
simplest ratio, so additional molar mass information is essential.
Check that the final formula reproduces the approximate percentages.
A balanced equation is a recipe in amounts of substance, not generally in
equal
masses.
Nitrogen plus three hydrogen molecules produces two ammonia molecules.
The same coefficients relate moles.
Start with two moles of nitrogen and three moles of hydrogen.
Divide each available amount by its reactant coefficient: nitrogen gives two,
while hydrogen gives one.
The smaller value identifies hydrogen as limiting.
One mole of nitrogen reacts with three moles of hydrogen, forming two moles of
ammonia and leaving one mole of nitrogen.
Using nitrogen fourteen and hydrogen one grams per mole, the initial masses
are
fifty six grams of nitrogen and six grams of hydrogen.
The products and remainder are thirty four grams of ammonia plus twenty eight
grams of nitrogen, again sixty two grams total.
A limiting reactant is not necessarily the one with the smaller mass or
smaller
raw mole amount.
Convert to moles and compare against the balanced coefficients.
This theoretical result assumes the stated reaction proceeds completely
without
competing chemistry.
Purity changes the amount of reactive material available before the reaction
starts.
Percentage yield compares the actual product obtained with the theoretical
product predicted from that available material.
Keep those two factors separate.
Imagine ten grams of limestone containing eighty percent calcium carbonate by
mass, with inert impurities.
The reactive calcium carbonate mass is eight grams.
On complete thermal decomposition, calcium carbonate gives calcium oxide and
carbon dioxide in a one to one mole ratio.
Using molar masses one hundred for calcium carbonate and forty four for carbon
dioxide, eight grams is zero point zero eight mole and predicts three point
five two grams of carbon dioxide.
If the actual recovered carbon dioxide is two point eight one six grams, the
percentage yield is eighty percent.
The original twenty percent impurity must not be subtracted a second time.
A measured yield above one hundred percent usually signals wet or impure
product, a mistaken assumption or measurement error, rather than creation of
extra matter.
State whether impurities react before treating them as inert.
For an ideal gas, pressure times volume equals amount times the gas constant
times absolute temperature.
Gas volume is therefore not a universal measure of moles unless temperature
and
pressure are specified.
At two hundred seventy three point one five kelvin and one atmosphere, one
mole
of ideal gas occupies about twenty two point four one litres.
At the same temperature and one bar, the value is about twenty two point seven
one litres.
Do not silently interchange these conventions.
Equal gas volumes at equal temperature and pressure contain equal amounts in
the ideal gas approximation.
For solutions, molarity is solute moles divided by solution volume in litres.
Zero point two zero mole in five hundred millilitres of solution gives zero
point four zero mole per litre.
During dilution without reaction or loss, solute amount stays constant, so
initial concentration times initial volume equals final concentration times
final volume.
Taking fifty millilitres of this solution and diluting to two hundred
millilitres gives zero point one zero mole per litre.
Use final solution volume, not merely the volume of water added.
A reliable mixed problem follows a chain of quantities with units attached.
Suppose five grams of a sample contains eighty percent magnesium by mass and
inert material.
Excess acid reacts with magnesium to give magnesium ions and hydrogen gas, one
mole of hydrogen per mole of magnesium.
With magnesium molar mass twenty four grams per mole, the reactive mass is
four
grams and the amount is one sixth of a mole.
At the stated ideal gas molar volume of twenty four litres per mole, complete
reaction predicts four litres of hydrogen.
If only seventy five percent of that theoretical gas is recovered, the
collected volume is three litres at those same conditions.
The acid is explicitly in excess; otherwise its amount would also need
checking.
Do not multiply by a percentage twice or apply a mass ratio directly as a mole
ratio.
Keep extra digits during calculation and round at the end according to the
supplied measurements.
Exact coefficients and entity definitions do not limit significant figures.
Use the practice questions to check each conversion before attempting longer
reaction chains.
A hydrate calculation uses the mole ratio of water to the anhydrous salt, not
the ratio of their measured masses.
Suppose supplied analysis says a two and one half gram hydrated copper sulfate
sample corresponds to one point six zero grams of anhydrous copper sulfate
after complete loss of water.
Assume only water is lost, no salt decomposes, and the sample has the stated
pure composition.
Water mass is zero point nine zero gram.
Using rounded molar masses eighteen for water and one hundred sixty grams per
mole for anhydrous copper sulfate gives zero point zero five zero mole water
and zero point zero one zero mole salt.
Their ratio is five, so the formula is copper sulfate with five waters of
crystallization.
The anhydrous formula unit remains the reference entity.
Incomplete water removal or loss of other material would invalidate the
interpretation.
A near integer ratio should be judged against the supplied measurement
precision rather than rounded aggressively from incompatible data.
This is interpretation of provided analytical results, not an instruction to
heat a substance without an appropriate supervised method.
Two independent measurements can determine a binary mixture when the reaction
model is specified.
Take a four point six four gram mixture containing only anhydrous sodium
carbonate and sodium hydrogen carbonate.
Complete reaction with sufficient strong acid gives two point two zero grams
of
carbon dioxide.
Using carbon dioxide molar mass forty four gives zero point zero five zero
mole
gas.
Each formula unit of either salt gives one carbon dioxide, so their mole
amounts a and b satisfy a plus b equals zero point zero five zero.
The mass equation is one hundred six a plus eighty four b equals four point
six
four.
Substitution gives a equals zero point zero two zero and b equals zero point
zero three zero mole.
The acid requirement is different: carbonate consumes two hydrogen ions per
formula unit, while hydrogen carbonate consumes one.
Total hydrogen ion consumption is therefore zero point zero seven zero mole.
Do not confuse equal gas coefficients with equal acid coefficients.
Check nonnegative amounts and reconstruct both total mass and gas yield before
accepting the solution; additional impurities or incomplete gas recovery
require a different model.
A reaction chain requires both stoichiometric coefficients and the yield of
each stage.
Consider the supplied abstract equations two A giving one B, followed by one B
giving three C.
Start with zero point one zero zero mole A.
At complete first stage conversion the theoretical B amount would be zero
point
zero five zero mole.
An eighty percent isolated first stage yield supplies zero point zero four
zero
mole B to the second stage.
That B could theoretically give zero point one two zero mole C.
A seventy five percent second stage yield therefore gives zero point zero nine
zero mole C.
Relative to the original A, the full ideal chain could have produced zero
point
one five zero mole C, so the overall yield is sixty percent.
Multiplying zero point eight by zero point seven five gives the same
fractional
result because the second yield is defined relative to the intermediate
actually supplied.
Do not add the percentages or apply both yields directly to the initial mole
amount while ignoring coefficient changes.
Side reactions, intermediate purity and recycled material need additional
information before this simplified chain model can be used.
Complete combustion products can reveal a hydrocarbon formula when the amount
of fuel is independently known.
Suppose zero point one zero zero mole of a pure hydrocarbon gives zero point
three zero zero mole carbon dioxide and zero point four zero zero mole water.
Each carbon dioxide contains one carbon atom, so each fuel molecule contains
three carbons.
Each water contains two hydrogen atoms, giving eight hydrogens per fuel
molecule.
The molecular formula is therefore C three H eight, not merely its carbon to
hydrogen empirical ratio.
The balanced combustion equation consumes five oxygen molecules per fuel
molecule, producing three carbon dioxide and four water molecules.
For the stated fuel amount, oxygen demand is zero point five zero zero mole.
Oxygen atoms in the products total one point zero zero mole of atoms,
equivalent to half that many moles of diatomic oxygen.
Keep atoms and molecules distinct.
This inference assumes complete combustion and quantitative product
accounting.
If the fuel contains oxygen or the starting fuel mole amount is unknown, the
same two product measurements alone require a different analysis.
Physical states also matter when converting product moles into measured gas
volumes.
Mass fraction, molarity and molality describe different denominators.
Take a supplied twenty point zero percent by mass sodium hydroxide solution
with density one point two zero grams per millilitre at the stated
temperature.
A one litre sample has total mass twelve hundred grams.
Twenty percent of that is two hundred forty grams sodium hydroxide, or six
point zero zero moles using molar mass forty.
Dividing by one litre gives six point zero zero molar.
The solvent mass is twelve hundred minus two hundred forty, or nine hundred
sixty grams.
Dividing six moles by zero point nine six zero kilogram solvent gives molality
six point two five moles per kilogram.
The two numerical concentrations are different because one denominator is
solution volume and the other solvent mass.
Density supplies the link between the given mass fraction and solution volume;
it does not justify assuming that volumes of solute and solvent add exactly.
Molarity depends on temperature through solution volume.
For this conversion use the density corresponding to the same specified
solution and temperature, and do not substitute solvent density for solution
density.
A back titration uses an excess reagent, then measures how much remains.
Suppose a one point zero zero gram sample contains calcium carbonate and an
impurity that does not consume acid.
The supplied acid amount is forty point zero millilitres of zero point five
zero zero molar hydrochloric acid.
After the carbonate reaction, the remaining acid consumes ten point zero
millilitres of zero point four zero zero molar sodium hydroxide in a
quantitative one to one neutralization.
Initial hydrogen ion amount is zero point zero two zero zero mole.
Remaining amount is zero point zero zero four zero zero mole, so the sample
consumed zero point zero one six zero mole.
Calcium carbonate needs two hydrogen ions per formula unit, giving zero point
zero zero eight zero zero mole carbonate.
With supplied molar mass one hundred grams per mole, its mass is zero point
eight zero zero gram and the sample purity is eighty percent.
This inference needs complete carbonate reaction, the stated acid inert
impurity and a valid residual acid endpoint.
Other acid consuming substances would change what the assay measures.
An oxide mixture can be solved from independent iron and oxygen balances.
Consider a supplied two point three two gram mixture containing only iron two
oxide and iron three oxide.
Complete reduction gives one point six eight grams iron, with all original
oxygen removed as water.
Use atomic masses iron fifty six and oxygen sixteen.
Iron amount is zero point zero three zero zero mole atoms.
The removed oxygen mass is zero point six four gram, corresponding to zero
point zero four zero zero mole oxygen atoms.
Let a and b be moles of iron two oxide and iron three oxide.
Iron balance gives a plus two b equal to zero point zero three zero zero.
Oxygen balance gives a plus three b equal to zero point zero four zero zero.
Subtraction gives b zero point zero one zero zero mole and then a the same
amount.
Their masses are zero point seven two zero and one point six zero grams.
The atom balances also predict zero point zero four zero zero mole water if
each removed oxygen forms one water molecule in the stipulated complete
reduction model.
An average atomic mass can give isotope number fractions under a stated two
isotope model.
Suppose chlorine has only mass thirty five and mass thirty seven isotopes,
with
supplied average mass thirty five point five.
If f is the heavy isotope fraction, thirty five times one minus f plus thirty
seven times f equals thirty five point five, giving f one quarter.
The light isotope fraction is three quarters.
For independent random pairing into diatomic chlorine, the light light
fraction
is nine sixteenths.
The mixed pair fraction is six sixteenths, because light heavy and heavy light
are two ways of obtaining the same mixed isotopologue.
The heavy heavy fraction is one sixteenth.
The molecular mass labels are seventy, seventy two and seventy four in this
integer mass model, and their weighted average is seventy one.
These are number fractions, not isotope mass fractions.
Actual isotope masses differ from integer mass numbers, and random pairing is
an explicit statistical assumption.
Identify the counted entity before transferring an atomic abundance directly
into a molecular peak ratio.
A binary hydrocarbon mixture needs both a total amount balance and a carbon
balance.
Suppose zero point one zero zero mole of a gas mixture contains only methane
and ethane.
Complete combustion produces zero point one six zero mole carbon dioxide.
Let a and b be the methane and ethane amounts.
The total balance is a plus b equal to zero point one zero zero.
Since methane contributes one carbon and ethane two, the carbon dioxide
balance
is a plus two b equal to zero point one six zero.
Therefore ethane is zero point zero six zero zero mole and methane zero point
zero four zero zero mole.
Their mole fractions are sixty and forty percent respectively.
Water production is two a plus three b, or zero point two six zero mole.
Oxygen demand is two a plus three point five b, or zero point two nine zero
mole.
With supplied molar masses sixteen and thirty, mean mixture molar mass is
twenty four point four grams per mole.
These results assume only the two named gases and complete formation of carbon
dioxide and water.
Parts per million is a ratio, so first identify whether the stated basis is
mass, volume or particle number.
On a mass basis, one part per million means one milligram solute per kilogram
of solution.
It is not automatically one milligram per litre.
Consider a supplied solution with solute mass concentration three point zero
zero milligrams per litre and density one point two zero kilograms per litre.
One litre therefore has solution mass one point two zero kilograms.
Dividing three milligrams by that mass gives two point five zero milligrams
per
kilogram, or two point five zero mass parts per million.
In a dilute aqueous solution whose density is approximately one kilogram per
litre, milligrams per litre can numerically approximate mass parts per
million,
but the density assumption must be stated.
Mass parts per billion use a factor of one billion instead of one million, so
one mass part per million equals one thousand mass parts per billion.
The denominator is the total solution mass, not just the solvent mass.
Keep the concentration basis attached to the number rather than using a trace
unit as a universal shortcut.
Gas mixture composition can be expressed in several different ways.
Suppose an ideal mixture contains two moles helium and one mole nitrogen
molecules at a common temperature.
The total amount is three moles, so the helium mole fraction is two thirds.
If the total pressure is three bar, Dalton's law gives a helium partial
pressure of two bar and nitrogen partial pressure of one bar.
With supplied molar masses four and twenty eight grams per mole, the helium
mass is eight grams and nitrogen mass twenty eight grams.
Helium therefore contributes only eight of the thirty six grams, a mass
fraction of two ninths rather than two thirds.
The mean molar mass is total mass divided by total amount, or twelve grams per
mole.
In the ideal gas model, density equals pressure times mean molar mass divided
by the gas constant and absolute temperature, using consistent units.
This relation can connect density to composition, but cannot uniquely identify
every possible mixture without knowing which gases are present.
Mole fraction counts chemical entities, whereas mass fraction weights each
entity by its molar mass.
A precipitation calculation starts with the ions that actually react rather
than every ion written in the molecular equation.
Mix twenty five point zero zero millilitres of zero point one zero zero molar
silver nitrate with forty point zero zero millilitres of zero point zero five
zero zero molar sodium chloride.
The initial silver ion amount is two point five zero millimoles and chloride
amount two point zero zero millimoles.
In the simplified complete precipitation model, the one to one net ionic
equation makes chloride limiting, giving two point zero zero millimoles silver
chloride.
Using the supplied molar mass one hundred forty three point five grams per
mole, the precipitate mass is zero point two eight seven gram.
Excess silver ion is zero point five zero zero millimole.
If final liquid volume is approximated by the sum, sixty five millilitres, its
excess silver concentration is about zero point zero zero seven six nine
molar.
Sodium and nitrate are spectator ions in this net reaction; they have not
disappeared from solution.
Finite solubility, complex formation and volume changes would require a more
detailed model.
State those approximations before treating the limiting ion result as exact
experimental recovery.
Atom economy is a supporting stoichiometric measure of how much reactant mass
enters the desired product in a balanced net reaction.
It differs from the percentage yield measured in a particular experiment.
Consider ethanoic acid plus ethanol forming ethyl ethanoate and water.
Use rounded molar masses sixty, forty six, eighty eight and eighteen grams per
mole, respectively.
One stoichiometric reaction unit starts with one hundred six grams of
reactants
and forms eighty eight grams of desired ester plus eighteen grams of water.
The ester atom economy is therefore eighty eight divided by one hundred six,
or
about eighty three point zero percent.
Even a hypothetical one hundred percent ester yield would not change that
stoichiometric fraction.
If an experiment starting with the stated stoichiometric amounts instead
isolates ester at eighty percent of theoretical yield, its ester mass is
seventy point four grams.
Product purity is yet another question: an impure recovered sample mass cannot
automatically be counted as pure ester.
This simplified atom economy calculation excludes solvents and other process
inputs and therefore does not measure every environmental impact or practical
waste stream.
Keep balanced reaction design, reaction yield and recovered sample purity as
separate quantities.
